subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Jet Stream and Blocking Patterns
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Jet Stream and Blocking Patterns.

hook.text: The jet stream is a river of fast wind 10 km above Earth. It steers weather across continents.

buildup.text: It flows west to east, driven by the temperature difference between the equator and the poles.

discovery.text: As the Arctic warms faster than the tropics, that temperature gap shrinks and the jet stream weakens.

twist.text: A weaker jet stream wobbles more, creating stuck weather patterns — prolonged heat or cold.

climax.text: These blocking patterns trapped the 2021 heat dome over the Pacific Northwest for days.

punchline.text: The wind that moves our weather is slowing down. Weather is getting stuck.

quiz.question: Why is the jet stream weakening?
options: The Arctic is warming faster, reducing the temperature gap

details.summary: The jet stream is a fast-flowing river of air at high altitude that steers weather systems across mid-latitudes. Arctic warming is weakening the jet stream, causing it to meander and stall, creating persistent weather patterns called blocking events that prolong heat waves and cold snaps.
details.whyItMatters: Blocking patterns turn ordinary weather into extreme events by holding heat waves, cold spells, or droughts in place for weeks. Their increase is one of the most consequential effects of Arctic warming.
takeaways: The jet stream flows from west to east at 150 to 300 km/h
Arctic amplification reduces the temperature gradient that drives the jet
Stalled jet-stream patterns caused the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome

faq.question: What is a blocking pattern?
faq.answer: A blocking pattern occurs when a large, persistent high-pressure system diverts the jet stream around it, preventing normal west-to-east weather progression. The block can hold heat waves or cold spells in place for days to weeks.

faq.question: How does Arctic warming weaken the jet stream?
faq.answer: The jet stream is driven by the temperature difference between the tropics and the Arctic. As the Arctic warms faster than the tropics, this gradient weakens, slowing the jet and causing it to take larger, slower-moving meanders.
